commentary.bottom_line: No study in this map tests whether contract terms requiring advance notice of vendor model changes, with updated model cards, change how health systems or clinicians detect or respond to those changes. Six sources endorse the practice, and two of them treat contract terms or documentation at procurement as the enforcement point.

perspectives.view: The map lists zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The support comes from six frameworks, guidance documents, and commentaries, which reflect expert consensus rather than measured outcomes. Under GRADE conventions, this body of support cannot be rated for certainty of effect, and the size or direction of any benefit is unknown.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software describes performance monitoring plans and transparency expectations for manufacturers, and the EU AI Act commentary calls for contract terms that require Annex XII documentation as a condition of supply. These sources suggest that contractual notice may extend regulatory transparency duties to the purchaser, though none reports whether such terms are honored.

No study in this map measures how often vendor model changes reach clinical use without notice, or whether such changes have altered outputs in ways that harmed patients. Without that data, the severity and frequency of the hazard remain unquantified, and no one has examined whether the practice intercepts errors before they reach patients.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems with and without contractual change-notice terms, measuring vendor compliance, time from model change to local awareness, the completeness of updated documentation, and whether local revalidation or clinician communication follows. Baseline data on how often unannounced vendor changes shift model outputs would also establish the size of the hazard.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. Safety-net systems may have less bargaining power in contract negotiations and fewer staff to review change notices, and whether the practice works for them is unknown.
